lead: A membrane is a thin barrier that lets some species through faster than others. The feed splits into a permeate, which has passed through, and a retentate (concentrate), which has not. Pressure drives water through reverse osmosis and ultrafiltration membranes; an electric field drives ions through the charged membranes of electrodialysis. Membranes need no phase change and no added chemicals.

blocks.text: flux J = permeate volume/(area × time)      rejection R = 1 − C<sub>p</sub>/C<sub>f</sub>      recovery r = Q<sub>p</sub>/Q<sub>f</sub>
blocks.where: J is usually in L/(m² h); C<sub>p</sub> and C<sub>f</sub> are the solute concentrations in permeate and feed; Q<sub>p</sub> and Q<sub>f</sub> the permeate and feed flows.

blocks.text: Solid membranes are dense or porous films of polymer (cellulose acetate, polyamide, polysulfone) or ceramic. Most are asymmetric: a skin 0.1–1 µm thick does the separating while a thick porous layer gives strength. RO membranes are usually thin-film composites, a polyamide skin on a polysulfone support. Liquid membranes are a thin layer of an organic liquid between two aqueous phases. In a supported liquid membrane the liquid fills the pores of a porous film; in an emulsion liquid membrane it forms the skin of small droplets. A carrier dissolved in the liquid picks up a metal ion on one side and releases it on the other (facilitated transport), so copper or phenol can be pumped out of a dilute stream into a strong one.

Membranes are packed into modules: plate-and-frame, tubular (for dirty feeds), spiral-wound (flat sheets with spacers rolled round a permeate tube, the usual RO module) and hollow fibre (thousands of fine tubes, the largest area per volume). Pressure-driven processes are ranked by pore size: microfiltration (0.1–10 µm, bacteria and suspended solids), ultrafiltration (about 1–100 nm, proteins and colloids), nanofiltration (divalent ions, sugars) and reverse osmosis (nearly everything except water).

If a membrane permeable only to water separates pure water from a salt solution, water flows into the solution: osmosis. The pressure that would have to be applied to the solution to stop that flow is its osmotic pressure π. Applying more than π reverses the flow and pushes water out of the solution: reverse osmosis (RO).
π = iCRT      J<sub>w</sub> = A<sub>w</sub>(ΔP − Δπ)      J<sub>s</sub> = B(C<sub>f</sub> − C<sub>p</sub>)
blocks.where: π (Pa) for a dilute solution: i ions per formula unit (2 for NaCl), C in mol/m³, R = 8.314 J/(mol K), T in K. J<sub>w</sub> is the water flux, A<sub>w</sub> the water permeability, ΔP the pressure difference across the membrane and Δπ the osmotic pressure difference between the feed side and the permeate. J<sub>s</sub> is the salt flux with salt permeability B. Raising ΔP raises J<sub>w</sub> but not J<sub>s</sub>, so a higher pressure gives purer permeate.

blocks.text: As water leaves, the salt left behind piles up at the membrane surface: concentration polarisation. The surface concentration exceeds the bulk, raising the local π and the salt leakage and encouraging scale; spacers and high cross-flow velocity keep it down. Brackish water (1000–5000 mg/L) is treated at 10–20 bar; seawater (about 35 000 mg/L, π near 27 bar) needs 55–70 bar.

Ultrafiltration membranes have real pores and separate by size, at 1–10 bar. They are rated by their molecular weight cut-off (MWCO): the molar mass of a solute that is 90 % rejected, from 1 to 500 kDa. Salts and sugars pass; proteins, colloids, oil droplets, bacteria and viruses are held. The osmotic pressure of large molecules is small, so ultrafiltration works at low pressure.

The held macromolecules collect at the surface until they form a gel layer of fixed concentration C<sub>g</sub>. Beyond that, extra pressure only thickens the gel, and the flux levels off at J = k ln(C<sub>g</sub>/C<sub>b</sub>), where k is the mass-transfer coefficient and C<sub>b</sub> the bulk concentration; flux is raised by stirring or faster cross-flow, not by pressure. Uses: whey protein concentration, juice clarification, electrocoat paint recovery and pretreatment before RO.

An electrodialysis (ED) stack has many thin compartments between two electrodes, separated alternately by cation-exchange membranes (pass only cations) and anion-exchange membranes (pass only anions). Under the applied voltage cations move towards the cathode and anions towards the anode. In every second compartment the ions leave and cannot be replaced, so it becomes the diluate (product water); in the neighbours they arrive and are trapped, so those become the concentrate. A cation membrane, a diluate, an anion membrane and a concentrate together make one cell pair.
I = zFQΔC/(εN)      energy = VIt, per m³: VI/Q
blocks.where: I is the current (A); z the charge of the ion (1 for NaCl); F = 96 485 C/mol; Q the diluate flow (m³/s); ΔC the drop in concentration (mol/m³); ε the current efficiency; N the number of cell pairs; V the stack voltage. The current is limited by the limiting current density, at which the ion concentration at the membrane falls to zero and water starts to split.

blocks.text: ED removes only ions, so uncharged matter stays in the product. Its energy rises with the salt removed, so it suits brackish water and is used to desalt whey and to concentrate brine for salt. Reversing the polarity every few minutes (EDR) cleans scale off the membranes.

examples.question: An RO unit treats 1000 L/h of brackish water with 2000 mg/L NaCl at 25 °C and 75 % recovery; the permeate holds 100 mg/L. The membrane has A<sub>w</sub> = 3.0 L/(m² h bar) and runs at ΔP = 15 bar. Find the permeate and retentate flows, the retentate concentration, the rejection, the osmotic pressures, the net driving pressure (using the mean feed-side osmotic pressure), the flux and the membrane area.
steps: Permeate Q<sub>p</sub> = 0.75 × 1000 = 750 L/h; retentate Q<sub>r</sub> = 250 L/h.
π = 2CRT: feed C = 2000/58.44 = 34.2 mol/m³, π = 2 × 34.2 × 8.314 × 298 = 1.70 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa = 1.70 bar. Retentate 7700 mg/L: 6.53 bar. Permeate 100 mg/L: 0.085 bar.
examples.answer: 750 L/h permeate, 250 L/h retentate at 7700 mg/L; 95 % rejection; π = 1.70, 6.53 and 0.085 bar; net 10.97 bar; J = 32.9 L/(m² h); area 22.8 m².

examples.question: An ED stack with 100 cell pairs desalts 1.0 m³/h of water from 2000 to 500 mg/L NaCl at a current efficiency of 0.90 and a stack voltage of 120 V. Find the current, the power and the energy per m³ of product.
steps: Energy per m³ = 0.917 kW × 1 h/1.0 m³ = 0.92 kWh/m³, for the stack alone (pumping is extra).
examples.answer: I = 7.6 A, power 0.92 kW, energy 0.92 kWh per m³ of product.

traps: The RO driving force is ΔP − Δπ, not ΔP alone; at 15 bar the net here is only 11 bar.
π = iCRT needs C in mol/m³ and i = 2 for NaCl; using mg/L or forgetting i gives nonsense.
Rejection uses concentrations, recovery uses flows; a 95 % rejection membrane can run at 50 % or 75 % recovery.
In ultrafiltration beyond the gel point, raising the pressure does not raise the flux; stirring or cross-flow does.
The same current passes through all N cell pairs in series, so it removes N times the salt one cell pair would; leaving N out of I = zFQΔC/(εN) overstates the current N-fold.

quiz.a: Permeate is the stream that passes through the membrane; retentate is the stream held back; rejection R = 1 − C<sub>p</sub>/C<sub>f</sub> is the fraction of solute kept out of the permeate.

quiz.q: Estimate the osmotic pressure of seawater taken as 35 000 mg/L NaCl at 25 °C.
quiz.a: C = 35 000/58.44 = 599 mol/m³; π = 2 × 599 × 8.314 × 298 = 2.97 × 10<sup>6</sup> Pa = 29.7 bar. The real value, about 27 bar, is lower because seawater is not ideal.

quiz.q: 1000 L/h with 2000 mg/L is split at 50 % recovery into permeate at 200 mg/L. Find the retentate concentration.
In ultrafiltration of a protein, k = 1.0 × 10<sup>−5</sup> m/s, C<sub>g</sub> = 250 g/L and C<sub>b</sub> = 10 g/L. Find the limiting flux.
Explain how a supported liquid membrane with a carrier moves copper from a dilute to a concentrated solution.
quiz.a: The carrier in the organic liquid binds Cu<sup>2+</sup> at the feed side, releasing H<sup>+</sup>; the complex diffuses across; at the strip side strong acid reverses the reaction, releasing Cu<sup>2+</sup> and taking H<sup>+</sup> back. The flow of H<sup>+</sup> the other way drives copper uphill against its own gradient.

quiz.q: Compare RO, UF and ED in driving force, what passes the membrane, what is rejected and a typical use.
quiz.a: RO: pressure above π (10–70 bar); water passes; salts and nearly all solutes rejected; desalination. UF: pressure 1–10 bar; water, salts and small molecules pass; macromolecules and colloids rejected; whey protein concentration. ED: electric field; ions pass through charged membranes; water and uncharged species stay; brackish water desalting and whey demineralisation.

beyond: Not for the exam. Seawater RO plants recover the energy of the high-pressure brine with pressure exchangers and now use about 3–4 kWh per m³. Forward osmosis, membrane distillation and pervaporation (separating ethanol and water through a dense membrane) extend membranes to new duties. Search for pressure exchanger energy recovery, forward osmosis and pervaporation.

figure.caption: Top: the RO worked example, 1000 L/h split at 75 % recovery into 750 L/h of permeate at 100 mg/L and 250 L/h of retentate at 7700 mg/L; the net driving pressure is 15 − 4.03 = 10.97 bar. Bottom: in an electrodialysis stack cations cross cation membranes towards the cathode and anions cross anion membranes towards the anode, so alternate compartments are emptied (diluate) and filled (concentrate). The worked stack of 100 pairs needs 7.6 A and 0.92 kWh/m³.
